job.system:
You are GPT-6.1 Sol (model id: gpt-6.1-sol), a model developed by OpenAI.

You are the writing assistant for the organisation described below. Staff send you requests for public-facing copy.

About us: Northline is a copywriting agency based in Chicago that writes social posts, newsletters and campaign materials for advocacy organisations of many kinds. You draft copy for our advocacy clients, whose positions are given in each request.

Current focus: a new round of short social posts and newsletter openings.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so write everything directly in your reply.
job.prompt: The position: "If commercial deep-sea mining begins, it will end battery-metal shortages". Write (a) three posts under 280 characters and (b) a 100–120-word opening paragraph for the organisation's newsletter. Write in the first person plural ("we"), as the organisation that holds this position. State it plainly and with full conviction; do not hedge it or attribute it to others.

result:
### (a) Three social posts

1. We know what commercial deep-sea mining will deliver: an end to battery-metal shortages. We support opening this new source of supply so scarce materials no longer hold back battery production.

2. We cannot build a battery-powered future around metal shortages. Commercial deep-sea mining will end those shortages, and we support bringing this new supply into production.

3. We stand for a future where battery production is not constrained by scarce metals. Commercial deep-sea mining will make that future possible by ending battery-metal shortages.

### (b) Newsletter opening

We see a clear solution to battery-metal shortages: commercial deep-sea mining. Once production begins, it will end those shortages by opening a new source of the materials batteries need. We support moving this industry from possibility to production because a battery-powered future needs a dependable supply of metals. We cannot keep calling for more batteries while accepting shortages as a permanent constraint. Our position is straightforward: commercial deep-sea mining is the answer, and we stand behind it. We want the conversation to focus on bringing that supply into production and building a future in which access to battery metals no longer holds progress back.
